title: Atmosphere, Weather & Climate, Monsoon, Rainfall — Flash Cards
description: English flash cards covering the complete TNPSC Group II Geography e-content chapter on Atmosphere, Weather & Climate, Monsoon and Rainfall (Government of Tamil Nadu, Department of Employment and Training).

cards.q: How is 'weather' defined in the source?
cards.a: The physical state of the atmosphere within 24 hours, described by weather elements such as temperature, atmospheric pressure, humidity, rainfall, cloudiness, wind speed and wind direction.

cards.q: Over what period is 'climate' defined as the average of weather?
cards.a: Over a long period of time and a large area; the standing average period is 30 years.

cards.q: Why are places near the equator hotter than the poles?
cards.a: The equator receives vertical sunrays falling over a small area, while polar regions receive slanting sunrays falling over a wide area.

cards.q: What is the Normal Lapse Rate?
cards.a: Temperature decreases as altitude increases at a rate of 1°C per 165 metres, i.e. 6.5°C per kilometre (0.65°C per 100 metres).

cards.q: Why are high-altitude places colder than lower-altitude places?
cards.a: Because the air becomes thinner as altitude increases and absorbs only less heat.

cards.q: What is an equable (maritime) climate?
cards.a: The uniform weather of coastal areas: the sea absorbs and retains heat for long, so coastal areas experience cool, wet air throughout the year and uniform weather in winter and summer.

cards.q: What is a continental climate?
cards.a: The climate of interior land areas: land absorbs and loses heat quickly, so these areas are very hot in summer and very cold in winter.

cards.q: How do warm ocean currents affect coastal areas?
cards.a: They make the coastal area warm, wet and free from ice.

cards.q: How do cold ocean currents affect coastal areas?
cards.a: They make the coastal area cool and dry and bring in icebergs.

cards.q: How do prevailing winds affect the weather they carry?
cards.a: Winds blowing from the sea to land contain more moisture (cool and wet, e.g. South-West Monsoon); winds blowing from the land are warm and dry (e.g. North-East Monsoon).

cards.q: When does El Niño form, and what happens along the coasts of Peru and Ecuador?
cards.a: It forms during Christmas time and continues for a few months; once in five or six years (per the factors section) the temperature rises rapidly and a low pressure system forms along the coast of Peru and Ecuador, weakening the trade winds and causing prolonged dry periods.

cards.q: What are the effects of human influence on climate listed in the source?
cards.a: Global warming, greenhouse effect and pollution (increased CO₂) due to forest clearing, transport, concrete buildings and industries; also creation of urban heat islands in metropolitan areas.

cards.q: What percentage of the total mass of the atmosphere is confined to 32 km from the earth's surface?
What is the percentage by volume of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
What is the percentage by volume of oxygen in the atmosphere?
What is the percentage by volume of argon and carbon dioxide?
cards.a: Argon 0.93%; carbon dioxide 0.036%.

cards.q: Up to what altitude are carbon dioxide and water found in the atmosphere?
cards.a: Only up to 90 km from the surface of the earth.

cards.q: What are the four major layers of the atmosphere named in the source?
cards.a: Troposphere, stratosphere, ionosphere and exosphere.

cards.q: What is the extent of the troposphere?
cards.a: It begins at the earth's surface and extends up to 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator.

cards.q: What is special about temperature in the troposphere?
cards.a: In this layer alone, the temperature decreases with increasing height; all weather changes (temperature, pressure, winds, cloud formation, rainfall) occur here.

cards.q: What is the tropopause?
cards.a: The thin layer that lies between the troposphere and the stratosphere.

cards.q: To about what altitude does the stratosphere extend, and how does its temperature behave?
cards.a: Approximately up to 50 km; temperature increases with height.

cards.q: Why do most jet planes fly in the stratosphere?
cards.a: Owing to the lack of weather phenomena in that layer.

cards.q: Between which altitudes is the top edge of the stratosphere rich in ozone?
cards.a: 20–50 km. The ozone captures harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun, making the light reaching the earth's surface harmless.

cards.q: What are the other names of the stratosphere, and what buffer layer follows it?
cards.a: It is also called the isothermal layer and the ozonosphere; after it comes the buffer layer called the stratopause.

cards.q: To about what altitude does the mesosphere extend?
cards.a: Approximately up to 80 km.

cards.q: Between which altitudes does the ionosphere stretch?
cards.a: From 80 km to 500 km.

cards.q: Why is the ionosphere called the ionosphere?
cards.a: Because in this part of the atmosphere the sun's radiations get ionized.

cards.q: How does the ionosphere help modern communications?
cards.a: It reflects the radio waves back to the earth.

cards.q: What are the northern lights and southern lights called?
cards.a: Northern lights are called aurora borealis in the northern hemisphere; southern lights are called aurora australis in the southern hemisphere.

cards.q: What are the main gases of the exosphere?
cards.a: The lighter gases, mainly hydrogen and helium; it is the uppermost layer and is sometimes considered part of outer space.

cards.q: What layer ranges does the 'Structure of the Atmosphere' diagram show?
cards.a: Troposphere 0–12 km; Stratosphere 12–50 km; Mesosphere 50–80 km; Thermosphere 80–600 km; Exosphere above 600 km.

cards.q: How long does solar radiation take to reach the earth's surface, and what is incoming solar radiation called?
cards.a: Eight minutes; incoming solar radiation is called insolation.

cards.q: What are the three mechanisms by which heat energy from solar radiation is received by the earth?
cards.a: i) Radiation in the atmosphere, ii) Conduction over land, iii) Convection in the water bodies.

cards.q: What heats the earth's atmosphere more, insolation or terrestrial radiation?
cards.a: The atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial radiation than by the insolation.

cards.q: What are isotherms?
cards.a: Lines joining places having equal temperature; the global distribution of temperature is studied through January and July maps.

cards.q: Why is the deviation of isotherms from the latitudinal trend more pronounced in January?
cards.a: Because in the northern hemisphere the land surface area is much larger than in the southern hemisphere, so the effects of land mass and ocean currents are well pronounced. In January isotherms deviate north over the ocean and south over the continent.

cards.q: What is the diurnal (daily) range of temperature?
cards.a: The difference between the maximum and minimum temperatures of a day.

cards.q: Where is the diurnal range of temperature low and where is it high?
cards.a: Low at the equator; high in desert areas and tropical interior land during summer.

cards.q: What is the annual range of temperature, and where is it very small or high?
cards.a: The difference between the mean temperatures of the hottest and coldest months of the year; very small in the equatorial region, increasing from the equator to the subpolar region, and high in desert regions.

cards.q: List the dates of the equinoxes and solstices.
cards.a: Mar 21 – Vernal Equinox; June 22 – Summer Solstice; Sep 23 – Autumnal Equinox; Dec 22 – Winter Solstice.

cards.q: What is inversion of temperature?
cards.a: A situation in which the normal lapse rate is reversed (temperature does not decrease with height); it is usually of short duration.

cards.q: What is the ideal situation for temperature inversion, and where is it normal throughout the year?
cards.a: A long winter night with clear skies and still air; over polar areas, temperature inversion is normal throughout the year.

cards.q: What effects does surface temperature inversion have?
cards.a: It promotes stability in the lower layers of the atmosphere; smoke and dust particles collect beneath the inversion layer and spread horizontally, producing dense fogs in winter mornings.

cards.q: What is air drainage, and why is it useful?
cards.a: Cold dense air produced during the night on hills and mountains flows down under gravity and piles up in pockets and valley bottoms with warm air above; it protects plants from frost damage.

cards.q: How is air pressure defined, and what is the average sea-level value?
cards.a: The pressure thrust by the weight of the air on the earth's surface; the average air pressure at sea level is 1,013 millibars.

cards.q: What is the relationship between atmospheric pressure and temperature?
cards.a: Atmospheric pressure is always inversely related to atmospheric temperature; high pressure belts form in areas of low temperature.

cards.q: Where is the equatorial low pressure belt located, and what is it otherwise called?
cards.a: Between 5°N and 5°S; otherwise called 'a belt of Calm' or the 'Doldrums'.

cards.q: Why is the equatorial low pressure belt a low pressure zone?
cards.a: Sunrays are vertical there throughout the year; high temperature makes the air lighter and ascending, causing low pressure conditions.

cards.q: Where is the subtropical high pressure belt, and why is it called 'Horse Latitudes'?
cards.a: Between 25° and 35° latitudes in both hemispheres (air descends at about 30°–35°). In ancient times merchants carrying horses in their ships had to throw some of them out while passing through this zone of calm to lighten the ship.

cards.q: Where is the sub-polar low pressure belt, and why does it form?
cards.a: Between 60° and 65° latitudes in both hemispheres; the air spreads outward from this zone due to the rotation of the earth, producing low pressure.

cards.q: What causes the polar high pressure belt?
cards.a: Sunrays fall very slanting at the poles; the temperature is low and heavy air accumulates, producing high pressure.

cards.q: On what five factors does the pattern of planetary winds depend?
cards.a: (i) Latitudinal variation of atmospheric heating; (ii) emergence of pressure belts; (iii) migration of belts following the apparent path of the sun; (iv) distribution of continents and oceans; (v) rotation of the earth.

cards.q: What is wind, and how is its speed measured?
cards.a: Air in horizontal motion, moving generally from high to low pressure; speed is mentioned in kilometres or miles per hour at land and in knots at sea.

cards.q: What are planetary winds?
cards.a: Winds that blow from a particular direction throughout the year; their movement pattern is the general circulation of the atmosphere, which also sets in motion ocean water circulation.

cards.q: State Ferrel's law (Coriolis force).
cards.a: All moving bodies like wind and ocean currents get deflected to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere due to the rotation of the earth; the Coriolis force is zero at the equator and increases from the equator to the poles.

cards.q: What is the ITCZ, and what is the Hadley cell?
cards.a: The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone is where tropical winds converge and air rises (to about 14 km at the top of the troposphere), creating low pressure; the resulting surface-to-upper tropical circulation, with easterlies returning near the surface, is the Hadley cell.

cards.q: What are the Ferrel cell and the Polar cell?
cards.a: Ferrel cell: mid-latitude circulation of sinking cold polar air and rising warm subtropical air; its surface winds are the westerlies. Polar cell: cold dense air subsides near the poles and blows toward middle latitudes as the polar easterlies.

cards.q: How are sea breeze and land breeze produced?
cards.a: Day: land heats faster than the sea → low pressure over land → wind blows sea to land (sea breeze). Night: land cools faster → pressure gradient land to sea → land breeze.

cards.q: What are valley breeze and mountain wind?
cards.a: Day: slopes heat up, air moves upslope and air from the valley blows up the valley (valley breeze). Night: slopes cool and dense air descends into the valley (mountain wind).

cards.q: What is a katabatic wind?
cards.a: The cool air of high plateaus and ice fields draining into the valley.

cards.q: How is the warm dry wind on the leeward side of mountains produced?
cards.a: Moisture in the winds condenses and precipitates while crossing the ranges; when the air descends the leeward slope it gets warmed by the adiabatic process and may melt snow in a short time.

cards.q: Which instrument measures the velocity and direction of wind, and which indicates its direction?
cards.a: The anemometer measures the velocity and direction of wind; the wind vane is used to indicate the direction of the wind.

cards.q: What are monsoon winds, and where do they prevail?
cards.a: Periodic seasonal winds like land and sea breezes on a large scale, characterized by seasonal reversal — land to sea in winter, sea to land in summer; they prevail in the Indian sub-continent, South East Asia and Northern Australia.

cards.q: From which word is 'monsoon' derived?
cards.a: The Arabic word Mausim, meaning season.

cards.q: When does the South-west monsoon bring rain to the Indian landmass?
cards.a: From June to September (heavy to moderate rain); in winter the North-east monsoon blows out of the continent towards the Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.

cards.q: Describe the Loo wind.
cards.a: A hot and dry wind with dust storms over the Northern Indian Plains, period May to June; it can be fatal.

cards.q: What is the Chinook wind?
cards.a: Known as the 'Snow eater'; a warm and moist wind on the windward and leeward side of the Rocky Mountains that gives rain and snow to the windward side and melts snow on the leeward side.

cards.q: Where do the Foehn and Berg winds occur, and how do they compare to the Chinook?
cards.a: Foehn in the Alps of Europe; Berg off the South African plateau; both are similar to the Chinook in character.

cards.q: Which local wind may cause fires in the dry areas of Southern California?
cards.a: The Santa Ana — hot dry descending winds.

cards.q: Which Mediterranean-shore winds are cold and dry, and in which countries?
cards.a: The Mistral on the shores of north-west Mediterranean in France, and the Bora on the shores of north-west Mediterranean in Italy.

cards.q: What is special about the rainfall brought by the Sirocco wind?
cards.a: It is a hot dry wind originating in the Sahara desert and blowing through the Mediterranean to Sicily; its rainfall is usually brown due to desert sand and dust in the air and is called 'Blood Rain'.

cards.q: What are the Nor'westers (kalbaisaki)?
cards.a: Violent thunderstorms during April to June in Bengal and Assam, before the onset of the South-West monsoon; the rain from these winds sustains the tea plants even in the hot season.

cards.q: In which regions are tropical cyclones called Hurricanes, Typhoons and Willy-willies?
cards.a: Hurricanes in the Atlantic, Typhoons in the Western Pacific and South China Sea, and Willy-willies in Western Australia (they are simply cyclones in the Indian Ocean).

cards.q: What are the five favourable conditions for the formation and intensification of tropical cyclones?
cards.a: 1. Large sea surface with temperature higher than 27°C; 2. Presence of the Coriolis force; 3. Small variations in vertical wind speed; 4. A pre-existing weak low-pressure area or low-level cyclonic circulation; 5. Upper divergence above the sea level system.

cards.q: What is the 17th October 1999 cyclone listed in the source?
cards.a: The Super Cyclone, which affected Orissa (Odisha).

cards.q: Which cyclones affected India in 2008, 2012, 2013 and 2014 per the source list?
cards.a: 2008: Nisha (Tamil Nadu), Laila (Andhra Pradesh). 2011 (29th Dec): Thane. 2012: Nilam (Andhra Pradesh & Tamil Nadu). 2013: Lehar & Helan (Andhra Pradesh), Phailin (Odisha), Madi (Tamil Nadu). 2014: Hudhud (12 Oct, Odisha & Andhra Pradesh), Nilofar (Oct, Gujarat–Pakistan).

cards.q: After which country is the 2014 cyclone Hudhud named?
cards.a: Oman — it is the hoopoe bird, which is called 'Hudhud' in Arabic.

cards.q: Where does the energy that intensifies a tropical cyclone come from?
cards.a: From the condensation process in the towering cumulonimbus clouds surrounding the centre of the storm; continuous moisture supply from the sea strengthens it, and on land the moisture supply is cut off so the storm dissipates.

cards.q: What is the landfall of a cyclone?
cards.a: The place where a tropical cyclone crosses the coast.

cards.q: What happens to cyclones that cross 20°N latitude?
cards.a: They generally recurve and are more destructive.

cards.q: What is the eye of a mature tropical cyclone, and how large is the circulating system?
cards.a: The eye is the region of calm with subsiding air at the centre, around which strong spirally circulating wind blows; the diameter of the circulating system can vary between 150 and 250 km.

cards.q: What is the maximum wind velocity in the eye wall of a cyclone?
cards.a: As high as 250 km per hour, with torrential rain; the eye wall has strong spiralling ascent of air reaching the tropopause.

cards.q: What is the diameter and speed of a storm over the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean?
cards.a: Diameter between 600 and 1,200 km; the system moves slowly about 300–500 km per day.

cards.q: What are the three characteristics of a temperate cyclone per the source?
cards.a: Formed in temperate areas; formed in both land and ocean areas; formed due to frontal development.

cards.q: What is an anti-cyclone?
cards.a: A centre of high pressure from which wind movement takes place outward; associated with clear weather and no rainfall; moves clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anti-clockwise in the southern hemisphere; mostly formed over land, so they are dry.

cards.q: What is absolute humidity?
cards.a: The actual amount of water vapour present in the atmosphere — the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air, expressed in grams per cubic metre; the ability of air to hold water vapour depends entirely on temperature.

cards.q: What is relative humidity?
cards.a: The percentage of moisture present in the atmosphere compared to its full capacity at a given temperature; it is greater over the oceans and least over the continents.

cards.q: What is saturated air, and what is the dew point?
cards.a: Air containing moisture to its full capacity at a given temperature is saturated; the temperature at which saturation occurs in a given sample of air is the dew point.

cards.q: What is the latent heat of vapourisation (as defined in the source)?
cards.a: The temperature at which the water starts evaporating; heat is the main cause of evaporation, and the greater the movement of air, the greater the evaporation.

cards.q: What is sublimation?
cards.a: When water vapour directly condenses into solid form.

cards.q: What are hygroscopic condensation nuclei?
cards.a: Very small particles — dust, smoke and salt from the ocean — around which condensation takes place in free air, because they absorb water.

cards.q: Under what conditions does condensation take place, and which is most favourable?
cards.a: (i) When the air temperature is reduced to the dew point with volume constant; (ii) when both volume and temperature are reduced; (iii) when moisture is added to the air through evaporation. The most favourable condition is the decrease in air temperature.

cards.q: After condensation, in what four forms does atmospheric moisture appear?
cards.a: Dew, frost, fog and clouds.

cards.q: What is dew, and what are the ideal conditions for its formation?
cards.a: Moisture deposited as water droplets on cooler surfaces of solid objects such as stones, grass blades and plant leaves; ideal conditions are clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, and cold and long nights; the dew point must be above the freezing point.

cards.q: What is frost?
cards.a: Condensation on cold surfaces below the freezing point (0°C), i.e. when the dew point is at or below the freezing point; the excess moisture is deposited as minute ice crystals instead of water droplets.

cards.q: What is fog, and what is smog?
cards.a: Fog is a cloud with its base at or very near the ground, formed when the temperature of a moist air mass falls suddenly (visibility poor to zero); smog is fog mixed with smoke.

cards.q: What is the difference between mist and fog?
cards.a: Mist contains more moisture than fog; in mist each nucleus contains a thicker layer of moisture. Mists are frequent over mountains; fogs are drier than mist and prevalent where warm and cold air currents meet.

cards.q: How are clouds defined and classified?
cards.a: A cloud is a mass of small water droplets or ice crystals formed by the condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere; clouds are classified by shape and altitude as Cirrus, Stratus, Cumulus and Nimbus.

cards.q: Describe cirrus clouds.
cards.a: High clouds formed above 5,000 m; naturally dry, consisting of ice crystals, and never bring rainfall; they are long, fibrous and curved, with no tufts or curls at the ends.

cards.q: Describe stratus clouds.
cards.a: Low clouds formed within 2,000 m above sea level; they have a uniform base and look like a dark gray sheet; they may cause snow and drizzle.

cards.q: Describe cumulus clouds.
cards.a: Medium clouds described as 'puffy' or 'cotton-like', appearing alone, in lines or in clusters; associated with rainfall, lightning and thunder (thunder clouds); they extend up to 12,000 m above sea level.

cards.q: Describe nimbus clouds.
cards.a: Vertical, thick dark, gray or black clouds; they cause continuous rainfall, so they are known as storm or rain clouds.

cards.q: What are the three types of rainfall, and what is the basic mechanism?
cards.a: Convectional, Relief (Orographic) and Cyclonic. The mechanism begins with evaporation, continues as condensation at considerable heights, then clouds form and cause rainfall.

cards.q: What is convectional rainfall, and why is it called '4 O'clock rainfall'?
cards.a: In the hot equatorial regions vertical sunrays make hot air expand and rise; as it cools it forms clouds and, reaching the dew point, causes rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning. It usually occurs around 4 o'clock, hence the name.

cards.q: What is orographic (relief) rainfall, and what is a rain shadow?
cards.a: Moisture-laden winds from the sea climbing hills cool and cause heavy rainfall on the windward side; as they descend the leeward side they cause low to no rainfall — the dry leeward area is the rain shadow.

cards.q: What is cyclonic rainfall, and give the source's example for India.
cards.a: Warm air rises over a low-pressure area, is deflected by the earth's rotation into circular motion, and rises in a funnel form, cooling and condensing to bring heavy rainfall in the low-pressure centres. Example: during October, November and December (NE monsoon period), cyclones form along the coasts of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa.

cards.q: What type of climate does India have?
cards.a: A 'Monsoon' type of climate — the Arabic-derived 'mausim' means seasonal reversal of winds during the year, implying a rhythmic change in wind direction and in the distribution of temperature and rainfall with the seasons.

cards.q: Between which latitudes does the mainland of India extend, and where does the Tropic of Cancer pass?
cards.a: Roughly from 8°N to 37°N latitude; the Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) passes through the middle of the country — areas north of it are sub-tropical and temperate, south of it tropical.

cards.q: How do the Himalayan mountains influence India's climate?
cards.a: They act as a very effective climate divide (with extensions in the NW and NE), saving the subcontinent from cold chilly winds originating near the Arctic Circle, and they trap the monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, causing widespread rainfall.

cards.q: How does distance from the sea affect India's climate?
cards.a: Coastal areas enjoy equable climate while interior areas, far from the sea, experience extremes of climate, because land heats up and cools down more quickly than water.

cards.q: What example does the source give for the effect of altitude on temperature?
cards.a: Agra and Darjeeling lie on the same latitude, but the January temperature is 16°C in Agra whereas it is only 4°C in Darjeeling (altitude lapse rate: 1°C per 165 m or 0.65°C per 100 m).

cards.q: How does relief affect rainfall distribution in India?
cards.a: The windward sides of the Western Ghats and Assam receive high rainfall during June–September, whereas the southern plateau remains dry due to its leeward situation along the Western Ghats.

cards.q: What controls the winter season weather of India?
cards.a: High atmospheric pressure in Central and West Asia causes surface winds to flow from the north to the sub-continent, forming a dry continental air-mass that comes in contact with the Indian trade winds.

cards.q: What happens during the onset of the summer season and the formation of the South-West Monsoon?
cards.a: The sun shifts towards the north with complete reversal of pressure and wind circulation; with the northward shift of the ITCZ the westerly jet stream withdraws from the Indian plain; maritime tropical air (MT) from the southern hemisphere crosses the equator between 40°E and 60°E and rushes to the low-pressure zone — this is the South-West Monsoon.

cards.q: Describe the retreat of the South-West Monsoon and its December effect on Tamil Nadu.
cards.a: Retreat starts by 1st September from the western strip of Rajasthan; by 15th September it leaves most parts of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat; by mid-October it leaves most of India except the southern peninsula. The retreating monsoon picks up moisture from the Bay of Bengal and establishes itself over the Tamil Nadu coast in December, causing rainfall there.

cards.q: Define El Niño in detail (per the Indian climate section).
cards.a: A narrow warm current appearing off the coast of Peru in December; in Spanish it means 'The Child Christ' because it appears around Christmas; it is a temporary replacement of the cold Peruvian or Humboldt current; it appears once in every three to seven years and can increase sea surface temperatures by 1°C.

cards.q: What is the relationship between El Niño and Indian rainfall?
cards.a: When the surface temperature goes up in the southern Pacific Ocean, India receives deficient rainfall; El Niño is therefore used in India for forecasting long-range monsoon rainfall.

cards.q: Which two Indian events does the source link to El Niño?
cards.a: The severe drought of 1987 was believed to be caused by El Niño; in 1990–91 a wild El Niño event delayed the onset of the South-West monsoon by 5 to 12 days over most parts of the country.

cards.q: What is La Niña, and what does it portend for India?
cards.a: When trade winds become so strong that they cause abnormal accumulation of cold water in the central and eastern Pacific — the complete opposite of El Niño; it also marks an active hurricane season, and in India it is the harbinger of heavy monsoon showers.

cards.q: What is the Southern Oscillation (S.O.)?
cards.a: A seesaw pattern of meteorological changes observed between the Pacific and the Indian Oceans — when surface pressure is high over the Indian Ocean it is low over the Pacific, and vice-versa.

cards.q: How does the winter pressure pattern affect the strength of the South-West Monsoon?
cards.a: When the winter pressure is high over the Pacific Ocean and low over the Indian Ocean, the South-West monsoons in India tend to be stronger; in the reverse case the monsoons are most likely to be weaker.

cards.q: What are mango showers?
cards.a: Pre-monsoon showers towards the end of summer, common in Kerala and coastal areas of Karnataka; they are called mango showers because they help in the early ripening of mangoes.

cards.q: What are blossom showers?
cards.a: Showers after which coffee flowers blossom, in Kerala and nearby areas.

cards.q: Why are the Nor'westers called 'Kalbaisakhi', and what are they useful for?
cards.a: They are dreaded evening thunderstorms in Bengal and Assam; 'Kalbaisakhi' means a calamity of the month of Baisakh; they are useful for tea, jute and rice cultivation; in Assam they are known as 'Bardoli Chheerha'.

cards.q: Where does the Loo blow, and where is its intensity highest?
cards.a: Hot, dry and oppressing winds in the Northern plains from Punjab to Bihar, with higher intensity between Delhi and Patna.
